web_evidence.title: It Can't Happen Here by Sinclair Lewis, from Project Gutenberg Canada
web_evidence.note: The complete text sustains external third-person narration from the opening through interior chapters and the ending, with access to Doremus's and other characters' thoughts. First-person passages are visibly delimited speech, documents, epigraphs, or dreams rather than an alternate base narrator.

web_evidence.title: It Can't Happen Here | Penguin Random House Secondary Education
web_evidence.note: The publisher's sustained extract externally narrates Doremus's movements, perceptions, and thoughts before and after an embedded first-person letter.

web_evidence.title: It Can't Happen Here Study Guide
web_evidence.note: The guide explicitly identifies a third-person omniscient narrator and distinguishes that grammatical narration from the frequent focalization through Doremus.

web_evidence.title: Sinclair Lewis Writing Styles in It Can't Happen Here
web_evidence.note: Its structural overview describes an omniscient perspective that ranges from Doremus-focused local events to national developments and occasionally other characters; these are focal shifts within third-person narration.

person_note: The Goodreads event passages repeatedly present Doremus, Windrip, Sarason, and other characters from a nonparticipating narratorial position, often reporting private beliefs or motives and ranging panoramically across national events. The complete text independently confirms that this third-person base continues from the opening through the interior and ending. Apparent first-person counterexamples are character speech or embedded propaganda, including q00135 from Windrip's Zero Hour and q00107, q00140, and q00156 from his Fifteen Points. Focalization shifts between Doremus, other characters, and national overview do not change grammatical person. No sustained first- or second-person base section was found; the remaining uncertainty is limited to clipped individual quotes, not the book-level structure.
